newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile airforce, navy look for Russian probe wreck.
newsitem.headline: Chile airforce, navy look for Russian probe wreck.

text.p: Chile's air force and navy combed the Pacific on Friday, looking for radioactive leaks and wreckage from a doomed Russian Mars robe following reports it may have crashed closer than thought to Chile's coast.
The air force sent a Hercules C-130 plane loaded with search equipment and radiation monitors and carrying nuclear energy experts to scour the waters off the port of Iquique, said military officials.

The search follows a report from NASA that a piece of the satellite, which was carrying eight ounces (200 grams) of plutonium, could have fallen in an area with its epicenter 20 nautical miles from Iquique.
Earlier reports had said the probe plunged into the depths of the Pacific Ocean hundreds of miles further east between the remote Easter Island and the Chilean mainland.
Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza reassured Chileans that they had nothing to fear from the accident, which happened nearly two weeks ago.
"We don't see any reason for public alarm or great concern. It is something we are investigating," said Insulza, adding that he had contacted the Russian ambassador in Santiago for more details.

Although most of the satellite burned up on re-entry, some of it probably survived, including four tiny canisters that contained enough plutonium to cause hundreds of cases of cancer if it came into contact with people, said U.S. scientists.
Three Chilean navy ships have sailed to the area to search the ocean bottom and take samples of the water to see if there are signs of any radiation leaks, said officials
Environmentalists have said that any radioactive contamination could devastate the rich fishing grounds in the southern Pacific that attract trawlers from around the world.
The probe plunged back to Earth the day after take-off after it failed to break out of the Earth's gravitational field when a rocket misfired.
